CHICAGO — Trade Show Executive’s (TSE) final Women to Watch spotlight of 2026 is on Brianne Somers, CEM, Senior Director of Exhibitions Services and The Utility Expo Show Director at the Association of Equipment Manufacturers (AEM).
p
Somers has expanded her influence across AEM’s full portfolio of major exhibitions and demonstrated operational excellence, purpose-driven leadership and executive decision-making under pressure.
p
For The Utility Expo, she supported and helped advance a strategy focused on enhancing the attendee experience while creating new opportunities for exhibitors, sponsors and industry partners.
p
We spoke with Somers about her impactful work — which includes helping The Utility Expo through unexpected flooding in 2025 — and leadership philosophy.
p
ANDREW: Can you tell us how you landed in the trade show industry and what has kept you here?
p
BRIANNE: I needed an internship to graduate, and my college had AEM on its list of recommended internship programs.
p

I saw a paid PR internship that somewhat aligned with my degree. While preparing for the interview, I actually had to Google what a trade show was. The hiring representative ultimately told me I was a better fit for the VIP Attendee Acquisition Internship, and here I am 10 years later.
p

I have stayed because working on a trade show of this scale, on behalf of an industry that serves such an important purpose, is genuinely fascinating. The people, the equipment and the complexity keep the work interesting.
p
ANDREW: Could you describe your work helping The Utility Expo 2025 succeed during severe flooding and what you learned from this experience?
p

BRIANNE: The biggest reason we successfully navigated the severe flooding at The Utility Expo 2025 was preparation. We had already done extensive crisis planning, worked through potential scenarios, established decision-making processes and prepared communications before arriving onsite.
p

When the flooding occurred, we relied heavily on our team, venue partners, public safety officials and other experts to guide decisions. My operations background helped me understand the potential impacts across the event, but the experience reinforced that the best decisions come from bringing the right people together and trusting their expertise.
p

What I learned most is that people respect decisions that prioritize safety, even when those decisions are difficult. Strong planning, clear governance and a team that trusts each other made all the difference.
p
ANDREW: What is your leadership philosophy, especially with complex cross-functional teams?
p
BRIANNE: My leadership philosophy is rooted in empathy, respect, transparency and culture. I care a lot about people and the environment we’re creating together.
p

In cross-functional environments, there are usually a lot of different perspectives in the room, and that’s actually a strength. I spend a lot of time listening, bringing people together and helping everyone stay focused on what we’re trying to accomplish.
p

I’ve found that when people understand the goal, feel heard and trust each other, they can work through just about any challenge. My role is usually to bring people together, create clarity and make sure everyone has what they need to be successful.
p
More than anything, I want to build teams where people enjoy working together, feel comfortable speaking up and know their contributions matter. That’s when the best work happens.
p
ANDREW: Could you describe your work championing The Utility Expo’s partnership with the American Foundation for Suicide Prevention (AFSP) and how it benefited the event?
p

BRIANNE: I was asked to create a social impact strategy for AEM’s tradeshow portfolio and identify a cause where our events could make a meaningful difference. As I dug into the research, I found that our social impact efforts had been focused on environmental sustainability.
p

While that’s incredibly important, sustainability had evolved into a core business practice in its own right, and I felt our social impact efforts should shift to focus on a different need facing the people who attend our events.
p
Through that research, I kept coming back to mental health. The construction industry had begun prioritizing mental health after data highlighted the alarming rate of suicide within the workforce.
p

At the same time, our content was already starting to tell that story, and I learned about the work the AFSP (American Foundation for Suicide Prevention) was doing alongside industry leaders to create construction-specific resources and support programs.
p
It felt like a place where we could make a real difference. We had a platform that could help get resources, education and awareness in front of the people who needed it most.
p

I also saw an opportunity to make this a portfolio-wide initiative so that our impact could extend beyond a single event. We launched the partnership at The Utility Expo, incorporating donations, education programming, resources, awareness campaigns and presentations on our Community Zone stage.
p

Many of the donations were made in honor of someone attendees had lost, and we heard so many personal stories throughout the event. Those conversations were incredibly moving and really validated that we had chosen an issue that deeply resonated with our audience.
p
The Utility Expo generated more than $24,000 in donations for AFSP, and we were able to build on that momentum at CONEXPO-CON/AGG, where the initiative generated more than $112,000.
p

We’re already planning additional initiatives for Utility Expo 2027, and I’m excited about the opportunity to keep expanding our support and hopefully make an even bigger difference within the industry.
p
ANDREW: What are some of the skills that have helped you move up in your organization, and how do you refine those skills?
p
BRIANNE: I think the skills that have helped me most are curiosity, strategic thinking, relationship building and staying calm when things get complicated.
p
Throughout my career, I’ve been willing to take on challenges that were outside my comfort zone and learn things I didn’t know much about.
p

That’s helped me develop the ability to see both the details and the bigger picture. On any given day, I might be working through an operational issue, reviewing a budget, talking with a customer or helping shape a long-term strategy, and I enjoy being able to connect all those pieces together.
p

I’ve also learned that relationships matter. Most of the work we do is highly cross-functional, so being able to build trust, listen to different perspectives and bring people together around a common goal has been incredibly important.
p

As for how I continue to grow, I try to stay curious. I ask for feedback, pay attention to what other events and industries are doing, spend time listening to exhibitors and attendees, and look for opportunities that continue to help me evolve.
p
ANDREW: What is your motivation to continue striving for excellence in your work?
p
BRIANNE: My kids are probably my biggest motivation. I want them to see the value of working hard, continuing to learn and always trying to do your best.
p
I’m also motivated by my team. I care a lot about helping people grow and creating an environment where we can do great work together. And honestly, I’m someone who enjoys a challenge.
p
I’m always looking for ways to learn, improve and make a bigger impact, which is what keeps me striving for excellence.
p

p
ANDREW: How do you maintain a healthy work-life balance to avoid burnout? How do you encourage others to do the same?
p
BRIANNE: My family is really what keeps me balanced. I have two young kids who are two and four, so when my workday is over, my focus shifts to them.
p
There are certainly busy periods where I’ll log back in after they go to bed, but I try not to make that the norm.
p
I’ve learned that you can’t pour from an empty cup. I believe in working smart and focusing on quality over quantity.
p
If I’m constantly working outside my normal hours just to keep up, that’s usually a sign that something bigger needs to be addressed.
p
I encourage my team to think about it the same way. Take your time off, be present with your family and don’t feel guilty about setting boundaries.
p
People do their best work when they’re energized, not when they’re running on empty.
p
ANDREW: How do you think women can support each other more in this industry? Or, in what ways do you think the trade show industry is evolving to better support women in leadership roles?
p
BRIANNE: I’ve been fortunate to have some incredibly supportive women throughout my career, and many of the values that shape my leadership philosophy today came from them.
p

The most meaningful support I received wasn’t necessarily from someone mentoring me directly. It was from women who said my name in rooms I wasn’t in, advocated for me when opportunities came up and then helped me prepare when those opportunities became a reality.
p
That’s probably the biggest way I think women can support each other. It’s not just opening doors, it’s helping each other walk through them successfully.
p

I also think our industry has made a lot of progress in creating more opportunities for women in leadership, but what has mattered most to me is seeing leaders who are willing to invest in other women, share their experiences and help build confidence along the way.
p
I’ve benefited from that support, and it’s something I try to pay forward whenever I can.
p
ANDREW: What do you think the next big thing in the events space is going to be?
p

BRIANNE: I think we’re going to see the industry really lean into technology, AI and data over the next several years. AI has the potential to create a lot of efficiencies and take some of the busy work off our plates, which gives event teams more space for creativity, strategic thinking and building better experiences.
p
I also think we’re just starting to scratch the surface when it comes to data.
p

We collect a tremendous amount of information, and I think the real opportunity is figuring out how to use that data to create value beyond the event itself. Whether it’s helping exhibitors better understand their customers, identifying industry trends or creating more personalized experiences, there’s a lot of potential there.
p
ANDREW: What strategies have you found most effective for building a strong professional network within the trade show community?
p
BRIANNE: Building your network is something you have to be intentional about. It’s not something you do once and check off the list.
p
I’ve gained some of my best ideas, advice and perspective from people in my network, and honestly, I can’t imagine doing this job without having that group of peers to learn from.
p
Whenever I have the opportunity to attend a roundtable, industry event, conference or networking function, I try to make time for it.
p

The education is always valuable, but the relationships are what I value most. Those are the people I can call when I’m working through a challenge, looking for a different perspective or trying to learn something new. Over time, those connections become one of the most valuable resources you have.
p
ANDREW: What role does mentorship play in your career development, and how can other women seek and cultivate these relationships?
p
BRIANNE: Mentorship has played a big role in my career, but I don’t think it always has to be formal. Some of the most valuable mentors I’ve had probably wouldn’t even call themselves mentors.
p
They’ve been leaders, peers and industry connections whose experience, advice or perspective helped me grow.
p
For other women, I’d encourage them not to wait for a formal mentorship program. Be curious, ask questions, build relationships and don’t be afraid to reach out to people you admire.
p

Most people are willing to share what they’ve learned if you take the initiative to start the conversation. Over time, those relationships can become some of the most valuable sources of support and growth in your career.
p
ANDREW: How do you stay updated on industry trends and changes, and what resources do you recommend to your peers?
p
BRIANNE: I read a lot, so books, articles and industry publications are a big part of how I stay current.
p

But I also pay attention to experiences outside of our industry. Whether it’s a baseball game, a theme park, Disney, a museum or even a movie theater, I’m always looking at how different organizations create experiences, engage customers and solve problems.
p

As I’ve moved into more leadership roles, I’ve also become more interested in broader trends like economics, geopolitics, technology and AI because they ultimately influence the industries our events serve.
p

But honestly, the most important thing I do is stay connected to our audience. I intentionally set aside time every week to read industry publications, watch videos and understand the challenges our attendees are dealing with.
p
If we’re going to create experiences that provide value, we need to understand what matters to them first.
